title: The growing importance of audit-ready taxpayer notification records
summary: Audits, appeals, and taxpayer inquiries all require one thing: documentation. Learn why tax offices are prioritizing audit-ready notification records.
body_text: Tax offices have always been responsible for more than collecting revenue. They are also responsible for maintaining the documentation that supports taxpayer communications, demonstrates compliance with notice requirements, and helps agencies respond to inquiries, appeals, audits, and public records requests. That responsibility is becoming increasingly important. As tax offices navigate staffing challenges, growing workloads, evolving technology expectations, and increased scrutiny around records management, many are taking a closer look at how taxpayer notifications are documented, retained, and retrieved. The conversation is no longer just about sending notices. It's about maintaining audit-ready records long after those notices have been delivered. Why Documentation Matters Long After a Notice Is Sent Every year, tax offices send thousands of important communications, including: Delinquent tax notices Tax lien notifications Assessment appeal decisions Collection notices Final notices before enforcement actions The operational task of sending these communications is often well-established. The bigger challenge frequently arises months—or even years—later. A taxpayer disputes receiving a notice. An auditor requests supporting documentation. An appeal requires proof that a communication was properly sent. A public records request requires access to historical mailing records. In these situations, the ability to quickly retrieve accurate documentation becomes just as important as the notice itself. The Record Behind the Notice When agencies think about taxpayer communications, the focus is often on the document being mailed. Equally important is the record that accompanies it. A complete taxpayer notification record may include: Proof of mailing USPS tracking history Delivery status Proof of receipt Date and time of delivery Supporting communication records Together, these records help establish a documented chain of evidence that can support compliance efforts and provide confidence when questions arise. Without a reliable system for maintaining and retrieving these records, agencies may find themselves spending valuable time searching for documentation that should be readily available. Preparing for Audits, Appeals, and Public Records Requests Tax offices are increasingly expected to provide timely responses to requests for information. Whether responding to: Internal audits External audits Taxpayer appeals Legal proceedings Public records requests staff often need access to historical communication records quickly and accurately. The challenge is that many agencies continue to rely on paper-based filing systems, physical storage, and manual recordkeeping processes. While these approaches may have served agencies well for years, they can make record retrieval time-consuming and resource intensive. When documentation is stored electronically and organized in a searchable format, agencies can respond more efficiently and with greater confidence. Compliance Is an Ongoing Responsibility Compliance doesn't end when a taxpayer notice is mailed. Many taxpayer communications are subject to statutory notice requirements, and agencies are often expected to maintain documentation demonstrating that notices were sent in accordance with established procedures. While requirements vary by jurisdiction, maintaining accurate records of mailing activity and delivery status can help support compliance efforts and provide valuable documentation during reviews, appeals, and audits. As expectations around transparency and accountability continue to grow, maintaining accessible communication records becomes increasingly important. The Hidden Costs of Manual Recordkeeping When discussing taxpayer notification processes, the conversation often centers on postage costs. However, the larger operational impact is frequently found elsewhere. Consider the time spent: Filing and storing records Retrieving historical documentation Responding to taxpayer inquiries Supporting appeals Preparing for audits Fulfilling public records requests Each task may seem minor in isolation, but collectively they can consume significant staff time over the course of a year. For agencies already managing limited resources, improving how records are maintained and retrieved can create meaningful operational benefits. Supporting Business Continuity Many tax offices depend on institutional knowledge accumulated over years—or decades—of service. Experienced employees often know exactly where records are stored, how notices were tracked, and which filing systems were used. But as retirements and staffing transitions continue across government, agencies are increasingly focused on preserving access to critical information. Centralized digital recordkeeping helps reduce dependence on individual employees by ensuring communication records remain accessible regardless of staffing changes. This supports both operational continuity and long-term records management objectives. Security and Trust Remain Critical Taxpayer communications often contain sensitive information related to property ownership, tax liabilities, payment history, and legal proceedings. As agencies evaluate technologies used to manage communication records, security should remain an important consideration. Solutions built on platforms with industry-recognized certifications such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001, as well as government-focused security frameworks aligned with NIST 800-53, can help agencies maintain confidence in the protection, integrity, and availability of taxpayer records. Moving Toward More Accessible, Audit-Ready Records Many agencies are modernizing how they manage taxpayer notification records through digital proof of mailing and delivery solutions such as Electronic Return Receipt (ERR). By replacing paper-based receipt management with searchable digital records, agencies can improve visibility into taxpayer communications while reducing the effort required to maintain and retrieve documentation. The result is not simply a more efficient mailing process. It's a more accessible, defensible, and audit-ready record of taxpayer communications. Looking Ahead As tax offices continue to balance compliance requirements, taxpayer service expectations, and resource constraints, the ability to quickly access accurate communication records will only become more important. The agencies best positioned for the future may not be those that send notices differently. They may be the ones that manage the records behind those notices more effectively. Because when questions arise months or years later, it's often the record—not the notice—that matters most. title: Budtender Incentives: Motivate Your Team and Lift Sales
summary: How budtender incentives boost dispensary sales and cut turnover, five plays you can run this week, and how Meadow and SparkPlug automate the whole thing.
body_text: Budtender incentives are structured rewards, such as contests, commissions, and brand-sponsored bonuses, that pay dispensary sales staff for hitting performance goals. Done well, they turn your front line into your growth engine: motivated budtenders sell more, learn products faster, and stay longer. The hard part has always been running them without drowning in spreadsheets. This guide breaks down why budtender incentives work, five incentive plays you can run this week, how to measure the results, and how the Meadow and SparkPlug integration automates the whole thing (free for Meadow clients for the first year). In This Post Why Budtender Incentives Work Five Budtender Incentive Plays What Incentives Actually Move Measure What's Working How the Meadow and SparkPlug Integration Works Common Questions Why Budtender Incentives Work Your budtenders shape what customers buy. In most transactions, the budtender is the deciding voice at the counter: the person who reads what a customer is after, steers an undecided shopper toward the right product, introduces something new, and turns a first visit into a repeat one. That makes staff motivation a direct lever on revenue, not a soft HR initiative. Incentives give that influence a direction. Put a reward on a specific product and budtenders have a reason to learn about it, start recommending it, and get sharper at selling it with every conversation. SparkPlug's co-founder and CEO, Andrew Duffy, frames the moment that matters: The moment when the customer's highest intent to purchase and most willing to try a new product is when they're standing right in front of the budtender at the counter. Leverage that opportunity to expose them to a new product and train your employees to sell them on products that might be a fit for the use case that they're describing. Andrew Duffy, Co-Founder and CEO of SparkPlug There's a retention story here too. Budtender turnover is one of the most expensive recurring costs in cannabis retail, between rehiring, retraining, and the product knowledge that walks out the door. Incentives give your best people a reason to stay: their skill shows up in their paycheck, not just in a manager's mental notes. Five Budtender Incentive Plays You can run every play below with a whiteboard and a spreadsheet. The manual version works; it just costs manager time and depends on someone remembering to tally, verify, and pay out. That is exactly the work the Meadow and SparkPlug integration automates, so each play notes where the integration takes over. 1. Hourly Flash Contests Pick a slow window, set a one-hour contest, and reward the budtender with the highest sales when the clock runs out. Resetting the clock each hour means multiple people can win in a day, which keeps the floor engaged instead of conceding to whoever started hot. Manually, this means a manager watching the register and tallying by hand. 2. Brand-Sponsored Product Promotions Run a competition on a specific brand or SKU you want to move. The budtender who sells the most wins, and everyone who participates learns the product well enough to recommend it. The unlock in cannabis retail: brands will often fund these rewards themselves, because counter recommendations are the most effective marketing they can buy. 💡 The Meadow x SparkPlug advantage: Brands you already carry sponsor incentives (SparkPlug calls them "Sparks") and pay the rewards directly, so you subsidize your team's pay without touching your own budget. You get notified when a brand offers a Spark and choose whether to accept. 3. Team Goals Set a collective sales target and reward the whole floor when they hit it. Team goals build camaraderie instead of rivalry, and they pull along staff who would never win a head-to-head contest but still contribute every shift. 4. Launch-Day Contests New product hitting the shelf? Run a contest on launch day. Your team learns the product fast because there's money on it, and the product gets recommended from day one instead of sitting on the shelf while staff get around to trying it. 5. Learn-and-Earn Training Rewards Pay staff to complete short product training, then follow with a sales contest on what they just learned. Education plus incentive beats either one alone: staff sell what they understand, and they understand what they were paid to study. 💡 The Meadow x SparkPlug advantage: SparkPlug's Courses feature pushes micro-training modules alongside incentive campaigns, so your team earns while they learn, and completion is tracked automatically. What Incentives Actually Move Structured, well-run incentive programs move the metrics dispensaries care about most: sales, retention, and customer experience. SparkPlug reports the following, based on its aggregate analysis of more than 250,000 incentive campaigns run across 4,000+ stores from 2020 through 2026: Turnover reduction is measured via POS employee profile turnover before and after implementing SparkPlug. SparkPlug is trusted by 3,000+ top cannabis brands and retailers. The two numbers to sit with are the first two. A sales lift pays for itself immediately, but a 30% drop in quarterly turnover compounds: every budtender you keep is a hiring cycle you skip and a regular customer relationship you don't reset to zero. Measure What's Working An incentive program you don't measure is just a payroll expense with extra steps. Whatever tool you use, a monthly check on three numbers is enough: Sales of the promoted product or category , before, during, and after each campaign, so you can separate real lift from a temporary spike. Per-budtender performance , including units per transaction and average basket size, to see who the incentives are actually motivating and who needs coaching instead. Turnover , quarter over quarter, since retention is where the quiet money is. 💡 How Meadow handles this: Meadow's staff performance reporting gives you the per-budtender view straight from the register, and SparkPlug's dashboards layer campaign results on top of it. How the Meadow and SparkPlug Integration Works The integration connects Meadow's POS to SparkPlug so every sale automatically counts toward active incentive campaigns, with no manual entry. Here's what that unlocks: Real-time POS sync: contests and goals run off live Meadow sales data, updating leaderboards and payouts automatically. Brand-funded rewards: most incentives are paid for by the cannabis brands you already carry. Automated tracking and fast payouts: budtenders claim rewards instantly via Venmo, Amazon, or Visa when they hit a goal. No spreadsheets, no end-of-day tallying. Runs inside the workflow: incentives surface as part of the normal selling flow, so staff engage without disrupting customer service. Rewards stay outside the product: payouts are cash or gift cards, never cannabis product. Incentive rules vary by state, so confirm specifics for your market with your compliance advisor. title: How Eliza Jennings Used CoreCare to Save Time, Prevent Write-Offs, and Improve Billing Accuracy
summary: CoreCare helps skilled nursing facilities collect every dollar with AI, proactively identifying and fixing eligibility, census, and compliance issues before
body_text: Overview Eliza Jennings is a nonprofit senior care network based in Northeast Ohio, with a 130-year legacy rooted in compassion and philanthropy. Founded by Eliza Jennings in the late 1800s as a “Home for Incurable Women,” the organization has grown into a trusted provider of skilled nursing, assisted living, and independent living across four facilities — all united by a mission to serve older adults with dignity and excellence. Challenge When Laura Banner, Director of Revenue Cycle Management, looked to strengthen financial accuracy across Medicaid operations, her team was already stretched thin. Before CoreCare, business office managers and billers at Eliza Jennings were mired in a highly manual verification process.Ohio’s state Medicaid portal required numerous keystrokes for each resident, and re-verifying eligibility monthly for a large Medicaid population consumed critical staff time. “The verification process was exhausting,” Banner recalled. “It took so many clicks just to confirm one resident’s benefits, and our team had dozens to review.” This burden was especially acute at the flagship Eliza Jennings Home, where 95% of residents are on Medicaid. “Sometimes we found out the hard way that someone had lost eligibility or changed managed care plans,” she explained. “Without enough time in the day, reverifications didn’t always happen. That created the risk of uncollectible revenue.” In several instances, residents were retroactively found ineligible, leaving the organization exposed to potential write-offs of $20,000 or more due to missing authorizations. Solution Having worked with CoreCare at a prior organization, Banner immediately recognized the value the platform could bring to Eliza Jennings. CoreCare’s automated verification technology replaced manual processes with customizable schedules and real-time alerts, providing immediate insight into eligibility changes, demographic mismatches, patient liability updates, and MCO transitions. Teams can access eligibility reports for an entire building in seconds—no more downloading PDFs and manually attaching them to each profile. “It’s like the everything bagel of Medicaid verification software,” said Banner. “We finally had everything in one place: eligibility alerts, program changes, patient liability, even demographic discrepancies. And it was all on one dashboard.” One early use case proved the platform’s value instantly. Banner recalled a time when a facility was operating without a dedicated business office manager. While regional staff tried to maintain coverage, CoreCare flagged that two Medicaid residents had lost eligibility. “In the past, that could have gone unnoticed until billing was processed,” Banner said. “Instead, CoreCare alerted us in real time. We were able to reapply for Medicaid immediately and avoid $20,000 to $30,000 in write offs.” At the Eliza Jennings Home, staff report saving at least 8 hours per month on Medicaid verification alone. By centralizing documentation and automating reverifications, team members reclaimed time previously spent clicking through state portals and manually tracking eligibility. This time savings has translated into more accurate billing and a stronger focus on collections. Banner noted, “We can now spot a patient liability change and immediately send an updated statement to the resident or their family. That keeps our revenue accurate and compliant.” Conclusion For a mission-driven nonprofit like Eliza Jennings, efficiency isn’t just about financial performance—it’s about protecting the resources that fund resident care. With CoreCare, the organization turned one of its most time consuming administrative tasks into a streamlined, automated process that saves hours each month and safeguards revenue. “CoreCare delivers exactly what we need—accurate data, time savings, and proactive alerts,” said Banner. “It’s been an incredibly helpful tool, especially for facilities with large Medicaid populations. The ROI is clear.”

title: Malos olores en casa: cómo eliminarlos | Hogarú en hogares y oficinas
body_text: Malos olores en casa: cómo eliminarlos y mantener un hogar fresco Publicado el 10 de Julio de 2026 por Equipo de crecimiento ¿Sientes un mal olor en casa y no sabes de dónde viene? Los malos olores en casa son un problema más común de lo que parece. Aunque limpies con frecuencia o uses ambientadores, algunos olores pueden permanecer durante días porque su origen está en lugares que suelen pasar desapercibidos, como los desagües, la basura, los muebles tapizados o la humedad. Además de resultar incómodos, los malos olores pueden hacer que el hogar se perciba menos limpio y confortable. La buena noticia es que, en la mayoría de los casos, es posible eliminarlos identificando su causa y adoptando una rutina de limpieza adecuada. En esta guía descubrirás: ✔️ Cuáles son las causas más comunes de los malos olores en casa. ✔️ Cómo identificar su origen. ✔️ Qué hacer para eliminarlos de forma efectiva. ✔️ Cómo prevenir que vuelvan a aparecer. ✔️ Cuándo una limpieza profunda puede ayudarte a mantener un hogar fresco y agradable. ¿Por qué aparecen los malos olores en casa? Los malos olores aparecen cuando se acumulan residuos, humedad, polvo o suciedad en diferentes espacios del hogar. En muchos casos, el origen del problema no está a la vista. Puede encontrarse en los desagües, los electrodomésticos, los textiles, las alfombras o incluso en el recipiente de la basura. La falta de ventilación, la presencia de mascotas y el exceso de humedad también favorecen la aparición de olores desagradables. Un consejo importante: los ambientadores solo ayudan a disimular el olor durante un tiempo. Para eliminarlo realmente, es necesario identificar y limpiar la fuente que lo produce. Las causas más comunes de los malos olores Existen diferentes lugares del hogar donde los malos olores suelen acumularse. Revisarlos con frecuencia y mantener una buena rutina de limpieza puede ayudarte a evitar que el problema empeore. 1. Basureros Los residuos orgánicos comienzan a descomponerse rápidamente, especialmente en climas cálidos. Cuando la basura permanece varios días dentro de la vivienda, es normal que aparezcan olores fuertes. ¿Qué puedes hacer? Vacía la basura todos los días. Lava el recipiente con agua y jabón regularmente. Utiliza bolsas resistentes y ciérralas correctamente. 2. Cocina La cocina es uno de los espacios donde más se concentran los malos olores. Los restos de comida, la grasa acumulada y algunos electrodomésticos pueden convertirse en una fuente constante de olores si no se limpian con frecuencia. No olvides limpiar: Nevera. Microondas. Horno. Lavaplatos. Campana extractora. 3. Desagües Los desagües de la cocina, el baño y el lavadero acumulan grasa, jabón, cabello y residuos que, con el tiempo, generan malos olores. Una limpieza periódica ayuda a evitar obstrucciones y mantiene los espacios con un aroma más agradable. 4. Sofás y muebles tapizados Aunque parezcan limpios, los muebles tapizados absorben polvo, humedad, restos de comida, sudor y olores provenientes de las mascotas. Aspirarlos con frecuencia y realizar una limpieza profunda periódicamente ayuda a conservarlos en buen estado y evita que retengan malos olores. 5. Alfombras y tapetes Las alfombras y los tapetes acumulan polvo, humedad, ácaros y otras partículas que no siempre son visibles. Si no se limpian regularmente, pueden convertirse en una de las principales fuentes de malos olores dentro del hogar. 6. Baño La humedad constante convierte al baño en uno de los lugares donde más fácilmente aparecen malos olores, especialmente cuando existe poca ventilación. Presta atención a la limpieza de: Inodoro. Lavamanos. Ducha. Cortina del baño. Desagües. 7. Mascotas Las mascotas hacen parte de la familia, pero también pueden dejar olores en camas, sofás, alfombras y otros textiles. Mantener una buena higiene tanto de ellas como de los espacios que utilizan ayuda a conservar un ambiente limpio y fresco. Cómo eliminar los malos olores en casa Si quieres eliminar los malos olores de forma duradera, lo más importante es actuar sobre la causa y no únicamente cubrirlos con fragancias. Estos hábitos pueden ayudarte: Ventila todos los días Abre puertas y ventanas entre 20 y 30 minutos para renovar el aire y reducir la humedad acumulada. Mantén una rutina de limpieza Eliminar el polvo, la grasa y los residuos evita que los olores se impregnen en los diferentes espacios del hogar. Lava los textiles periódicamente Las cortinas, cobijas, cojines, fundas y alfombras también acumulan polvo y olores con el paso del tiempo. No acumules la basura Sacar la basura diariamente evita que los residuos comiencen a descomponerse dentro de la vivienda. Controla la humedad Revisa posibles filtraciones y procura mantener secos los espacios con poca ventilación. Errores que hacen que los malos olores vuelvan A veces el olor desaparece por unos días y luego regresa. Esto suele ocurrir por algunos hábitos muy comunes. Evita : Usar únicamente ambientadores. No ventilar la vivienda. Olvidar limpiar los desagües. No lavar sofás ni alfombras. Dejar acumular la basura durante varios días. Ignorar problemas de humedad. ¿Cada cuánto deberías hacer una limpieza para evitar malos olores? Mantener una rutina constante ayuda a prevenir que los olores reaparezcan. Como referencia general: Tarea Frecuencia recomendada Sacar la basura Todos los días Limpiar la cocina Todos los días Limpiar el baño Una vez por semana Aspirar sofás y alfombras Una vez por semana Lavar cortinas y otros textiles Cada 2 o 3 meses Realizar una limpieza profunda Cada 6 meses ¿Cuándo necesitas una limpieza profesional? Hay ocasiones en las que los malos olores persisten incluso después de realizar la limpieza habitual. Esto puede ocurrir cuando: Los muebles conservan olores impregnados. Existe acumulación de grasa en la cocina. Hay problemas de humedad. El polvo lleva meses acumulándose. La vivienda estuvo desocupada durante un largo periodo. En estos casos, una limpieza profunda profesional permite llegar a zonas difíciles de alcanzar y eliminar la suciedad que suele pasar desapercibida. Beneficios de eliminar los malos olores Mantener un hogar libre de malos olores no solo mejora la percepción de limpieza. También aporta beneficios para el bienestar diario. Entre ellos: Un ambiente más fresco y agradable. Mayor sensación de limpieza. Menor acumulación de humedad y suciedad. Espacios más cómodos para compartir en familia. Un hogar más acogedor para recibir visitas. Preguntas frecuentes ¿Por qué mi casa huele mal aunque esté limpia? El origen puede encontrarse en lugares que no siempre forman parte de la limpieza diaria, como desagües, muebles tapizados, alfombras, electrodomésticos o problemas de humedad. ¿Los ambientadores eliminan los malos olores? No. Los ambientadores ayudan a disimular los olores de forma temporal, pero no eliminan la causa que los produce. ¿Cómo evitar que los malos olores regresen? Ventila tu hogar todos los días, mantén una rutina de limpieza constante, controla la humedad y realiza limpiezas profundas de manera periódica. ¿Cada cuánto se recomienda hacer una limpieza profunda? Aunque depende del uso de la vivienda, realizar una limpieza profunda aproximadamente cada seis meses ayuda a mantener un hogar limpio, fresco y en mejores condiciones. ¿Quieres disfrutar de un hogar limpio y con un ambiente fresco? Mantener una casa libre de malos olores requiere constancia y una limpieza adecuada. Sin embargo, hay momentos en los que la suciedad acumulada necesita una atención más profunda. En Hogarú contamos con profesionales capacitados para ayudarte a limpiar esas zonas que suelen pasar desapercibidas en el día a día, eliminando la suciedad acumulada y contribuyendo a mantener un ambiente más limpio y agradable. Ya sea una limpieza profunda o un servicio de aseo regular, estamos listos para darte una mano. ¿Necesitas una mano? title: Receive webhooks in OpenClaw and Hermes
summary: Two new open-source plugins let OpenClaw and Hermes agents receive webhooks without a public webhook endpoint.
body_text: Svix is the enterprise ready webhooks sending service. With Svix, you can build a secure, reliable, and scalable webhook platform in minutes for both sending and receiving them . Want webhooks in your product without building the hard parts yourself? Give it a try! Trying to get your agents to consume webhooks is a huge pain. You have to run an HTTP endpoint, make sure to have a dynamic DNS, open ports in the router, and watch out for webhooks failing every time you close your laptop or have internet issues. I knew there must be a better way so I built a plugin that solves all of that using Svix and makes receiving webhooks a breeze! Receiving webhooks in your agent sucks Traditionally when someone wants to inform you of an event, they make an HTTP request to a URL you gave it. That works great when 'you' are a server with a stable public address. AI agents usually aren't on a stable address because often they run on a laptop, a dev environment behind a VPN, inside a locked corporate network, or in some kind of sandbox that can't accept inbound traffic. To take webhooks the normal way, that agent has to expose either a public URL, an open port, or a tunnel. That's annoying to set up and in a lot of environments it's a no-go for security reasons. How Svix enables agents to consume webhooks The trick is to flip the direction of the connection: instead of the webhook provider pushing events to your agent, your agent pulls them from Svix. Svix Ingest is the first step: you paste a Svix Ingest URL into whatever platform you want events from, and Svix takes it from there. It verifies the signature and buffers every message until your agent comes to collect them, without any additional infrastructure on your side. The second step is creating an AutoConfig polling token and adding it to your agent plugin config. AutoConfig is a single token that lets the plugin provision its own polling endpoint and start pulling messages, no dashboard setup needed. The plugin polls over a plain outbound HTTPS connection (every 5 seconds by default) and commits its position as it goes, so nothing on your side ever needs to be reachable from the internet. This is also what solves the closed-laptop problem from earlier: if your agent is offline, messages simply queue up in Svix, and the next poll picks up exactly where the last one left off. Nothing gets dropped. OpenClaw The OpenClaw plugin turns incoming webhooks into actions on your agent: a webhook arrives at Svix, and on the next poll your agent creates a flow, runs a task, or wakes up. Under the hood it maps polled messages onto OpenClaw's existing webhook surface, either as TaskFlow actions ( create_flow , run_task , …) against a bound session, or as gateway hooks POST ed to OpenClaw's documented /hooks/wake / /hooks/agent endpoints. Three steps: Clone the repo and link the plugin into your OpenClaw install: git clone https://github.com/svix/ai.git openclaw plugins install --link ./ai/plugins/svix-openclaw Add a route under plugins.entries.svix-openclaw.config.routes . Each route gets a single AutoConfig token (no URL to set) and the session its actions apply to: { "routes": { "ops": { "token": { "source": "env", "provider": "env", "id": "SVIX_TASKFLOW_AUTOCONFIG_TOKEN" }, "sessionKey": "agent:main", }, }, } Run the gateway ( openclaw gateway ). Anything sent to that route's Ingest URL gets applied as an action on the next poll, e.g.: { "action": "create_flow", "goal": "Investigate alert" } Point your alerting system at the route's Ingest URL and that payload is all it takes: the alert fires, and a few seconds later your agent is already investigating it. Hermes The Hermes plugin turns incoming webhooks into prompts for your agent, and delivers the agent's response wherever you want it. It follows the same shape as Hermes' built-in webhook adapter, so each event flows through the familiar route → prompt → delivery pipeline. Three steps: Clone the repo and install the plugin and the Svix SDK: git clone https://github.com/svix/ai.git cp -r ai/plugins/svix-hermes ~/.hermes/plugins/svix-hermes pip install 'svix>=1.96.0' Add a route under platforms.svix.extra.routes in your gateway config.yaml . Give it an AutoConfig token, a prompt template, and a delivery target: platforms : svix : enabled : true extra : routes : github_events : token_env : SVIX_GITHUB_AUTOCONFIG_TOKEN prompt : "GitHub issue opened: {issue.title}\n\n{__raw__}" deliver : telegram deliver_extra : chat_id : '123456789' # your Telegram chat id Start the gateway. Each route provisions its sink on the first poll, then drains it from there. No other setup needed. With the route above, someone opens an issue on your repo and a few seconds later your agent messages you on Telegram about it. No server, no tunnel, no open ports.
